title: He Walked Into the Clinic Talking, Yet Scans Showed His Self Network in Deep Anesthesia
description:
Behavioral & Circuit Analysis — Jules Cotard (1880) & Berrios (1995): Cotard's Nihilistic Delusion — When the Brain Insists You No Longer Exist, grounded in G. E. Berrios, R. Luque (1995) (Acta Psychiatrica Scandinavica). Empirical findings show that on June 28, 1880 in Paris, neurologist Jules Cotard presented 'Mademoiselle X', a 43-year-old woman with severe agitated melancholia who calmly insisted she possessed 'no brain, no nerves, no chest, no stomach, and no intestines' — only skin and bones — and paradoxically concluded that because she had no organs, she could never die naturally and had zero need to eat.

At the circuit level, this episode examines how insula, default mode network, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex coordinate behavioral and neural responses, alongside evidence that cotard named this condition le délire des négations ('delirium of negation'), noting it ranged from denying a single internal organ or emotion all the way to denying one's own name, age, family, or physical existence altogether.

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- G. E. Berrios, R. Luque (1995). Cotard's syndrome: analysis of 100 cases. Acta Psychiatrica Scandinavica. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1600-0447.1995.tb09764.x
- Andrew W. Young, Ian H. Robertson, Deborah J. Hellawell, Karel W. de Pauw, Brian Pentland (1992). Cotard delusion after brain injury. Psychological Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1017/s003329170003823x
- O. Hantkie (2009). Jules Cotard: sa vie, son œuvre. PSN. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11836-009-0082-6

AI Disclosure: Visual reenactments, 3D anatomical models, and narration in this documentary Short were produced with AI synthesis tools from verified peer-reviewed sources.
